tip: English sees an action (they are sitting); Spanish sees a state: 'están sentados' = they are seated. 'Están sentándose' would mean they're in the very act of lowering themselves into chairs.
'Ser' for scheduled events: 'La reunión es a las diez'.
'Hay un mapa' asks whether one exists at all; '¿Está el mapa?' would ask about one specific, known map. Existence pairs 'hay' with 'un' – a known thing takes 'estar' with 'el'.
'El problema' ends in '-a' but is masculine (Greek origin: '-ema', '-ama').
'Escribirse' = to write to each other. The 'se' here is reciprocal: 'Nos escribimos' = we write to each other.
'Cuesta' agrees with the T-shirt, not with you – the item is the subject doing the costing. Shopping for two things? '¿Cuánto cuestan?' The question pluralizes along with the goods.
'Estar harto de' = to be fed up with. 'Estar' is used for emotional/temporary states, not 'ser'.
'Los domingos' = on Sundays (definite article + day = habitual).
'Para' = for (recipient): 'Este regalo es para ti.' 'Para' marks who receives something.
'Estar' + 'listo' = ready (temporary). 'Ser' + 'listo' = clever (inherent trait).
'Fijarse en' = to notice: 'me fijo en los detalles' = I notice the details. Always reflexive + 'en'.
'Acostar' is to put someone to bed; the 'se' in 'se acuestan' bends it back – the kids put themselves to bed.
Spanish drops 'a' before jobs: 'es médico', never 'es un médico'. The article only returns when you add an adjective – 'es un médico excelente'.
'Dejar' + infinitive = let something happen: 'no dejan pasar la luz'. Note the order – 'la luz' comes after 'pasar', the reverse of English 'let the light through.'
For dates Spanish asks where you 'are' on the calendar: '¿A cuánto estamos?' 'Estamos a veintiséis' – literally 'we're at the 26th' of the month.
'¿Recibiste?' – one email, one moment of arrival, done. If you can pin an action to a single point in time, preterite is your tense; ongoing or habitual would need imperfect.
In Spanish the preposition leads the question: '¿De dónde eres?' opens with 'de' (from), literally 'from where are you'.
'¿Por qué?' (two words, with accent) = why? 'porque' (one word, no accent) = because. The accent and spacing matter.
English says 'at' the university; Spanish reaches for 'en', as if you study inside the institution: 'estudio en la universidad'. Same with 'en la oficina', 'en la escuela'.
'La foto' – feminine because it's short for 'la fotografía'. Shortened words keep the gender of the full word.
Why plural? Spanish greetings come in plural: 'Buenos días' = literally 'good days'. Same logic for 'buenas tardes' and 'buenas noches' – always plural.
'Llevar' + time = to have been (doing something) for (duration). 'Llevo dos años aquí' = I've been here for two years. Very common construction.
'Tus' is plural because 'padres' is plural – not because of how many 'yous' there are. Spanish possessives agree with the thing owned: 'tu padre', 'tus padres', same one owner.
Dogs 'call themselves' in Spanish. Names use 'llamarse': '¿Cómo se llama tu perro?' = literally 'How does your dog call himself?' – 'cómo', never 'qué'.
Note 'otra vez': 'otro/a' never takes an indefinite article – it's 'otra vez', never 'una otra vez'.
'Mi mujer' = literally 'my woman' – and the everyday word for 'wife' in Spain. 'Mujer' means wife only with a possessive ('mi mujer', 'la mujer de Juan'); 'esposa' is the safe-everywhere word.
'¿Cómo?' means 'how?' with accent. Without accent, 'como' means 'like/as' or 'I eat.'
'La mano' is feminine – one of very few '-o' nouns that are feminine. Memorize it as an exception.
'El planeta' is masculine. Many '-a' words from Greek/Latin are masculine: 'planeta', 'problema', 'mapa'.
'Por' for duration: 'Estudié por dos horas.' 'Por' marks how long something lasted.
